clue.text: Communication at a distance peculiar to India and Africa?

definitions.text: Communication at a distance peculiar to India and Africa?

parts.words: Communication at a distance peculiar to India and Africa?
parts.note: a long-distance telephone call read whimsically as a call made by the elephants of India and Africa, which trumpet through their trunks

explanation.surface: A question about some form of long-distance messaging found only in India and Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: The old British term for a long-distance phone call becomes, read literally, the trumpeting of an elephant, the beast of India and Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: An old British phrase for a long-distance telephone call, booked through the operator.

clue.text: Rabble coming up to tour duke's house

indicators.note: to tour is to go round, so one piece travels around the other
in a down clue, coming up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a rout is an old word for a disorderly crowd or rabble
D is the abbreviation for duke

explanation.surface: A mob arriving to look round a nobleman's stately home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming up' turns ROUT into TUOR, and 'to tour' puts D inside it. The house is the royal dynasty, not a building.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tudors were a royal dynasty, and a dynasty is called a house, as in the House of Windsor.

clue.text: Gun exploded, sounding strangely outrageous

indicators.note: something exploded is blown apart, so the letters of the gun are scattered
sounding means the next piece is a word said out loud and spelt as it sounds

parts.note: strangely means in an odd way

explanation.surface: A gun goes off and makes a peculiar and shocking noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exploded' rearranges GUN into UNG; 'sounding' asks for a spelling that says 'oddly', ODLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Ungodly is used informally for something outrageous or unreasonable, as in an ungodly hour.

clue.text: It heightens the division between motorist and pedestrian

definitions.text: It heightens the division between motorist and pedestrian

parts.words: It heightens the division between motorist and pedestrian
parts.note: read as social tension, but literally the raised edging stone that lifts the pavement above the road

explanation.surface: Something that worsens the rift between drivers and walkers.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests worsening hostility; literally the stone raises the pavement's edge above the road.
explanation.definitionFit: A kerbstone (British spelling of curbstone) forms the raised edge between road and pavement.

clue.text: Taking turns to put new heart into N argument

indicators.note: to put means one letter is placed where another stood
heart into means the central letter of the word is the one that is swapped

parts.note: an altercation is a noisy argument

explanation.surface: Instructions to swap in a fresh core for a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: The central letter of ALTERCATION is C; 'to put' and 'heart into' replace it with N. The stray 'N' in the held clue is an OCR slip for 'an'.
explanation.definitionFit: Alternation is the act of doing things by turns, one after another.

clue.text: It can be read as impertinence

definitions.text: It can be read as impertinence

parts.words: It can be read as impertinence
parts.note: a mouth's shape can be read by the deaf, and the same word is slang for cheek or backchat

explanation.surface: Something that may be taken to be cheekiness.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a remark taken the wrong way; the hint is lip-reading, and the word is also slang for cheek.
explanation.definitionFit: Lip is informal for impudent talk, and lips are what lip-readers read.

clue.text: Confronted by coffee sent back

indicators.note: sent back means the word is turned round and read from end to start

parts.note: decaf is decaffeinated coffee

explanation.surface: Someone faced with a coffee that was returned to the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sent back' reads DECAF backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To be faced with something is to be confronted by it; both are past forms of a verb.

clue.text: Ground for discussion may come from ref or umpire

indicators.note: may come from means the letters are taken out of a run of the clue's words

explanation.surface: An argument on the pitch arising from a match official.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may come from' takes the answer out of 'reF OR UMpire'. 'Ground' suggests a sports field.
explanation.definitionFit: A forum is a place or setting for public debate, a ground in the sense of venue.

clue.text: Shortly appear to appeal over fine in B Roman assembly

indicators.note: shortly means cut short, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: to come is to appear or arrive
it is slang for sex appeal

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means the piece is turned up the other way

parts.note: A1 means first-rate or fine, with the digit read as the letter I

explanation.surface: Briefly turning up to lodge an appeal against a penalty before a Roman body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shortly' cuts COME to COM; 'over' turns AI (from A1) into IA. The held 'B' is an OCR slip for 'a'.
explanation.definitionFit: The comitia were the legislative and electoral assemblies of the people of ancient Rome.

clue.text: Multilateral arrangement where God and deacon differ

indicators.note: where two words differ, their letters are set out in a different order

explanation.surface: A church dispute in which a deacon disagrees with the divine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'differ' rearranges GOD and DEACON.
explanation.definitionFit: A dodecagon is a figure with twelve sides, so it is a many-sided shape.

clue.text: Trail revolutionary follower at a gentle pace

parts.note: to dog someone is to trail or follow them
a Trot is a follower of the revolutionary Trotsky

explanation.surface: A Marxist tracked down by someone strolling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A dogtrot is a steady easy jog, a gentle running pace.

clue.text: Funeral pile almost in the middle of tomb

indicators.note: almost means the word stops one letter short of the end

parts.note: a pyre is a pile of wood on which a body is burnt
amid means in the middle of

explanation.surface: A burial heap sitting nearly at the centre of a grave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims PYRE to PYR.
explanation.definitionFit: The Egyptian pyramids were built as tombs for the pharaohs.

clue.text: Resolution originally put before mid- March is carried

indicators.note: put before means the first piece stands ahead of the next
originally points to the very start of the word

parts.note: the Ides of March fell in the middle of the month, on the fifteenth

explanation.surface: A motion first tabled in mid-March is passed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'originally' picks the first letter of 'Resolution'. 'is carried' looks like the motion passing; it is a passenger travelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who rides is borne along on a horse or vehicle, so is carried.

clue.text: Room joined to attic, say, with rickety steps

indicators.note: say means the words are only spoken, and spelt another way

parts.note: the words room and attic run together form the spoken sound

explanation.surface: A room linked to a loft, reached by a shaky staircase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' asks for a word that sounds like 'room-attic'. 'rickety steps' looks like a staircase, but it is a person's stiff gait.
explanation.definitionFit: A rheumatic person has aching joints and so walks unsteadily.

clue.text: Manoeuvring locomotive over point on loop

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means the first piece sits above the next
on means the next piece follows directly

parts.note: a locomotive is a railway engine
E is east, one of the compass points
a ring is a loop or circle

explanation.surface: A train shunted across a set of points onto a loop line.
explanation.walkthrough: The railway picture hides compass 'point' E.
explanation.definitionFit: Engineering can mean contriving or manoeuvring to bring something about, as in engineering a meeting.

clue.text: Period with Lewis as poet

definitions.meaning: Cecil ...-Lewis was a poet laureate, whose surname combines this word with Lewis

explanation.surface: A spell when Lewis served as a poet.
explanation.definitionFit: A day is a span of time, and joined to Lewis it names the poet laureate Cecil Day-Lewis.

clue.text: Lifted cue shot — that's cheating

indicators.note: shot means wrecked or ruined, so the letters are broken up and reordered

explanation.surface: A snooker player raises the cue for a stroke and is accused of foul play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shot' looks like a snooker stroke; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Deceitful means dishonest or misleading, so cheating.

clue.text: Go on a university grant to work for Primate

indicators.note: to work letters is to work them into a new shape

explanation.surface: Advice to take a student grant, aimed at a church leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to work' rearranges GO ON A, U and GRANT. 'Primate' suggests an archbishop; it is the ape.
explanation.definitionFit: The orang-utan is a great ape of Borneo and Sumatra, and apes are primates.

clue.text: Can't be kept down: sure to win, though bowled out early on

indicators.note: out early on means a letter near the start of the word is dropped

parts.note: unbeatable means sure to win
B is the cricket abbreviation for bowled

explanation.surface: A cricket team seems invincible but is dismissed early in its innings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out early on' removes B from UNBEATABLE. 'Can't be kept down' is about food the stomach rejects.
explanation.definitionFit: Food that cannot be eaten, or would not stay down, is uneatable.

clue.text: A comfort for gentlemen

parts.note: a comfort or amenity, and the gentlemen's public toilet sign in Britain

explanation.surface: Some ease or luxury provided for men.
explanation.walkthrough: A public convenience is the British euphemism for a public toilet, labelled Gentlemen.
explanation.definitionFit: Convenience means comfort or amenity, and a public convenience is a British toilet.

clue.text: So-called token

definitions.meaning: token means small and symbolic, as a token payment

explanation.surface: A payment that is merely a gesture.
explanation.definitionFit: Nominal means existing in name only, and also very small, as a nominal fee.

clue.text: Preserve in container

definitions.meaning: to preserve food by sealing it in tins

explanation.surface: Keeping food in a jar.
explanation.definitionFit: To can food is to preserve it, and a can is a metal container.

clue.text: Published and won

definitions.meaning: a newspaper that ran a story has published it
a motion that won the vote passed

explanation.surface: An article went to print and took a prize.
explanation.definitionFit: A paper carries a story when it prints it, and a motion is carried when it wins the vote.

clue.text: Coming soon, in Mice and Men movie

indicators.note: movie read as something that moves, so the letters are shifted about

explanation.surface: A trailer advertising a new film adaptation of the Steinbeck novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'movie' looks like a film; read as 'moving', it rearranges IN, MICE and MEN; 'and' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Imminence is the state of being about to happen, of coming soon.

clue.text: Impossible not to get on with her?

definitions.text: Impossible not to get on with her?

parts.words: Impossible not to get on with her?
parts.note: the British exclamation of refusal 'not on your ...', meaning no chance, read as a woman too amiable to fall out with

explanation.surface: A woman so pleasant that everyone gets on with her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not on your nelly' is British slang for 'certainly not'; the clue reads 'not on' as 'not get on'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'not on your nelly' expresses an emphatic refusal, implying something is impossible.

clue.text: The weights of packaging produce sound of rips

indicators.note: sound of means a word that is heard the same but spelt differently

parts.note: tears are rips in fabric

explanation.surface: Heavy wrapping makes a tearing noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'produce' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A tare is the weight of a container or wrapping, deducted to find the net weight.

clue.text: Saw noisily installed

indicators.note: noisily means the word is spoken, not written

parts.note: to have sighted something is to have seen it

explanation.surface: A carpenter's saw was set up with a racket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' is a verb here, as in spotted, not the tool.
explanation.definitionFit: Sited means placed or positioned in a location, so installed.

clue.text: Cool bash for groupies

parts.note: to fan something is to cool it
to club is to bash or hit

explanation.surface: A trendy party for devotees of a band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cool' and 'bash' are verbs, not the adjective and party.
explanation.definitionFit: Groupies are devoted fans, the kind who make up a fan club.

clue.text: Robert has to bow

definitions.meaning: A short form of the name Robert

explanation.surface: A man called Robert is obliged to bend at the waist.
explanation.definitionFit: Bob is a nickname for Robert, and a bob is a quick bow or curtsy.

clue.text: Integral unit one pound off

indicators.note: off means gone wrong, so the letters are set in a new order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
lb is the abbreviation for a pound weight

explanation.surface: A whole unit with a pound deducted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' rearranges UNIT, I and LB.
explanation.definitionFit: Something inbuilt is integral, forming part of the structure itself.

clue.text: Money for a sticky sweet

definitions.meaning: a lollipop, a sweet on a stick

explanation.surface: Paying for a sugary treat.
explanation.definitionFit: Lolly is British slang for cash and also short for lollipop, a sweet on a stick.

clue.text: Conceited journalist is after major source

indicators.note: is after means the next piece follows the earlier ones

parts.note: big means major or large
the head of a river is its source
ED is short for editor, a journalist

explanation.surface: A self-important reporter chasing a big-name informant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'source' suggests a news contact; it is a river's head.
explanation.definitionFit: Big-headed means conceited, full of oneself.
